column4: ## Old Covenant Washings - Historical Context
column5: ## Washings in the Old Covenant - Historical Background

column4: In the Old Covenant, ceremonial washings played a central role in maintaining ritual purity and symbolizing holiness before God. These washings were prescribed in the Law of Moses and applied both to the priests who served in the Tabernacle and to the people of Israel. For example, priests were required to wash their hands and feet at the bronze basin before entering the Tabernacle or approaching the altar, symbolizing their readiness to serve in the presence of a holy God (Exodus 30:18-21). Similarly, rituals for cleansing individuals from defilement, such as contact with a dead body or skin diseases, involved washing with water as a sign of restoration to purity (Leviticus 14:8; Numbers 19:17-19). These acts served as outward demonstrations of an inward desire for holiness, emphasizing the importance of being set apart for God.
column5: In the Old Covenant, ritual washings played a central role in maintaining purity in worship and symbolizing holiness before God. These washings were prescribed in the Law of Moses and applied both to the priests who served in the tabernacle and to the people of Israel. For example, the priests were required to wash their hands and feet at the bronze basin before entering the tabernacle or approaching the altar. This symbolized that they were prepared to minister before the Holy God (Exodus 30:18-21). Likewise, purification rites from uncleanness associated with touching a corpse or with skin diseases included washing with water, which signified the restoration of purity (Leviticus 14:8; Numbers 19:17-19). These acts outwardly expressed the desire for inward holiness and underscored the importance of being set apart for God.

column4: The ceremonial washings in the Old Testament required regular repetition to maintain ritual purity. Unlike permanent solutions, these rituals only provided temporary external cleansing, leaving the deeper issue of sin unresolved. The writer of Hebrews highlights this limitation, explaining that these practices were “symbolic for the present time,” unable to clear the conscience of the worshiper (Hebrews 9:9-10). These washings acted as constant reminders of human imperfection and the need for something greater-an ultimate purification that could cleanse not just the body, but the heart and soul as well.
column5: The ritual washings in the Old Testament had to be performed repeatedly to maintain ceremonial purity in worship. Unlike a permanent solution, these rites provided only temporary, external cleansing and left the deeper issue of sin unresolved. The author of Hebrews highlights this limitation, stating that these practices were “symbols for the present time” and could not cleanse the worshipers’ conscience (Hebrews 9:9-10). These washings continually reminded people of human imperfection and of the need for something greater—the ultimate purification—namely, something that could cleanse not only the body but also the heart and soul.

column4: The ceremonial washings of the Old Covenant find their fulfillment in Christ, who provides complete and eternal cleansing through His sacrifice. Unlike the temporary rituals of the law, Christ’s blood purifies fully, cleansing not just the flesh but also the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14). Through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplished what the Old Testament rituals could only foreshadow-true reconciliation with God. Hebrews 10:22 calls believers to “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” This language ties Christ’s work to the imagery of Old Testament washings while showing its far superior efficacy. His sacrifice does not merely cover sin but removes it completely (1 John 1:7). In this way, the ceremonial washings served as a shadow, pointing to the deeper cleansing that only Christ could provide, fulfilling humanity’s need for holiness through divine intervention.

Unlike the temporary rites of the law, the blood of Christ cleanses fully, purifying not only the body but also the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14). Through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplished what the Old Testament rites foreshadowed as a shadow—true reconciliation with God. Hebrews 10:22 exhorts us to draw near to God with the full assurance of faith, as those who have had our hearts sprinkled to cleanse an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. Christ’s sacrifice does not merely cover sin; it completely removes it (1 John 1:7). Thus, the ritual washings served as shadows pointing to the deeper cleansing that only Christ can give, through which God’s intervention meets humanity’s need for holiness.

column4: John the Baptist’s ministry centered on preparing the way for the coming of Jesus Christ. His baptism, described as a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Mark 1:4), called people to confess their sins, turn their hearts back to God, and prepare for the arrival of the Messiah. It served as an outward sign of inward repentance, symbolizing a desire for spiritual cleansing and readiness for the kingdom of God. John’s baptism, however, was temporary and preparatory-it pointed forward to the greater work that Christ would accomplish. While John’s baptism focused on repentance, it did not provide complete forgiveness or spiritual regeneration, as it lacked the indwelling and empowerment of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11-12). Instead, John openly declared that one greater than He was coming, who would baptize not only with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16).

However, John’s baptism was temporary and preparatory, pointing to the greater work that Christ would accomplish. Rather, John openly declared that One greater than he would come, who would baptize not only with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16).

column4: John’s baptism was fulfilled and surpassed through the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Christian baptism, instituted by Jesus and practiced by the apostles, signifies a deeper reality-union with Christ, death to sin, and resurrection to new life (Romans 6:3-4). Unlike John’s baptism, Christian baptism is directly connected to faith in Jesus’ atoning sacrifice and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38). The arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost marked the new covenant and the beginning of Spirit-empowered living, which John’s baptism could not provide. Because of this, John’s baptism is no longer practiced, as it has been replaced by the baptism commanded by Christ (Matthew 28:19), which incorporates repentance, faith, and the sealing of believers by the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13-14).

For this reason, John’s baptism is no longer practiced; it has been replaced by the baptism commanded by Christ (Matthew 28:19), which encompasses repentance, faith, and the Spirit’s sealing of the believer (Ephesians 1:13-14).

column4: ## Christ’s Baptism
column5: ## Christ’s Baptism

column4: Christ’s baptism set a powerful example for His followers and established the foundation for the Christian practice of water baptism. Though Jesus was without sin, He submitted to baptism by John to “fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). In doing so, He identified with humanity’s need for repentance and pointed forward to His own death, burial, and resurrection. At His baptism, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father declared, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16-17). This moment marked the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry and revealed the unity of the Father, Son, and Spirit, foreshadowing the spiritual transformation believers would experience through faith in Christ.
column5: Christ’s baptism served as a powerful example to the disciples and laid the foundation for water baptism in Christianity. Though sinless, Jesus submitted to be baptized by John “to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). In doing so, Jesus identified with humanity’s need for repentance and foreshadowed His own death, burial, and resurrection. At His baptism, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father declared, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16-17). This event marked the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry, revealed the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, and foreshadowed the spiritual transformation believers experience through faith in Christ.

column4: Jesus later commanded His followers to be baptized, commissioning them to “go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Water baptism, as instituted by Christ, became an **act of obedience** and a **public declaration of faith** for believers. It represents their identification with Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4). Going under the water symbolizes dying to sin, and coming up out of the water illustrates rising to new life in Christ (Colossians 2:12). Yet, it is crucial to clarify that this outward act is not the source of salvation but a **visible sign** of the **inner work of grace** already accomplished by the blood of Jesus.

column4: Water baptism is a **symbol** of the cleansing power of Christ’s blood and the renewal of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:26; Titus 3:5). It signifies repentance, faith, and a commitment to follow Jesus. It is an outward testimony of an inward transformation-a way for believers to publicly declare their allegiance to Christ and their participation in the body of Christ, the Church (Acts 2:41). While it is commanded by Jesus and modeled in the early Church, it does not **save** a person. Salvation is by grace through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8-9), and the true cleansing occurs spiritually through the blood of Christ (Revelation 1:5). Water baptism is a response to that salvation, an act of obedience rather than a requirement for it.

column4: In the New Testament, water baptism is consistently tied to **repentance and faith** (Acts 2:38; Mark 16:16), both of which require a personal decision to follow Christ-something infants are not capable of making. Baptism symbolizes a believer’s deliberate identification with Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4), as well as their commitment to live in obedience to Him. Some denominations (e.g., Catholics, Lutherans) practice infant baptism as a covenantal sign akin to circumcision, however because infants cannot express personal faith or repentance, the practice of **infant baptism** does not align with the biblical model of **believer’s baptism**. Instead, many churches practice **dedication ceremonies** for infants, following the example of Hannah dedicating Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:27-28) and Mary and Joseph presenting Jesus at the temple (Luke 2:22). Dedication is not a substitute for baptism but rather a commitment by parents to raise their child in the faith, teaching them God’s Word, and modeling a godly life until the child is old enough to make their own decision to follow Christ and be baptized.

column4: ## Holy Spirit Baptism
column5: ## Baptism of the Holy Spirit

column4: The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a profound and transformative experience promised by God to empower believers for ministry, service, and holy living. Every believer receives the Holy Spirit when they’re born again-this is how we’re made spiritually alive. But later, we should also receive the baptism in the Holy Spirit, which empowers us for boldness, spiritual gifts, and effective ministry.

column4: Water baptism is a public declaration of faith and symbolizes the cleansing of sin through Christ’s blood, Spirit baptism represents the empowering presence of God in the believer’s life. Together, these two modes of baptism form complementary aspects of the Christian walk-one as an outward sign of obedience and the other as an inward source of power and renewal. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is the Spirit upon us rather than within. At salvation all believers receive the Spirit within them, but when the Spirit of God comes upon them, they receive power and boldness for ministry.

column5: ## How to receive the baptism in the Holy Spirit

column4: The baptism of the Holy Spirit is described in Scripture as a gift that is promised to believers and is received by faith. It is separate from salvation and is primarily for empowerment and witness (Acts 1:8). The baptism of the Holy Spirit is a gift of empowerment for believers, promised by Jesus and fulfilled at Pentecost. It is received through repentance, faith, and asking God. While laying on of hands is often used as a method, it is ultimately God who baptizes with the Spirit.

It is distinct from salvation and is primarily for endowment and witness (Acts 1:8). The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a gift of power to believers, promised by Jesus and fulfilled at Pentecost. It is received through repentance and faith, and by asking God. The laying on of hands is often used as a means, but ultimately it is God Himself who administers the baptism in the Holy Spirit.

column4: Scripture presents speaking in tongues and prophecy as a common sign, but the purpose of this baptism is far greater-providing boldness, power, and spiritual gifts for ministry.
